hooks.text: One of our giant planets was once named George.
Why was the planet Uranus almost named after a king?
The world we call Uranus was once named George.

title: The Planet That Was Almost a King
description: William Herschel tried to name the first planet discovered since antiquity after King George III, sparking a global scientific feud.

beats.text: One of our giant planets was once named George.
beats.visual: Uranus natural color photograph from Voyager 2 mission, 1986

beats.text: Musician William Herschel found this giant world in his back garden.
beats.visual: Portrait of astronomer William Herschel by Lemuel Francis Abbott, 1785

beats.text: He discovered it with a homemade telescope and named it after King George.
beats.visual: Portrait of King George III of the United Kingdom by Allan Ramsay, 1762

beats.text: The King gave him a salary, but other scientists were absolutely furious.
beats.visual: Antique 18th century map of the Solar System showing planetary orbits

beats.text: They refused to let a British monarch sit among the ancient gods.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Roman god Uranus in a celestial setting

beats.text: French astronomers even spent years calling the planet Herschel instead.
beats.visual: Engraving of William Herschel's seven-foot reflecting telescope used for his discovery

beats.text: Everyone finally agreed on Uranus to keep the mythological names consistent.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope natural color image of Uranus showing its thin rings

beats.text: It remains the only world that was almost a king.
beats.visual: Portrait of King George III of the United Kingdom in coronation robes
